summary:
Official WorldPride Amsterdam 2026 safety and travel guidance states that visa requirements for the Netherlands depend on nationality alone. Transgender and non-binary visitors are not treated differently in visa applications, and a passport carrying a gender marker other than the one assigned at birth, or an 'X' marker, is accepted for entry provided it was officially issued. No additional gender documentation may be demanded at the border.

Discrimination on grounds of gender identity is prohibited. Gender expression became an explicitly protected ground under the Equal Treatment Act in March 2019, following passage by the House of Representatives in 2018 (127 votes to 23) and the Senate on 12 March 2019 (64 to 11), after the Netherlands Institute for Human Rights had already treated transgender people as covered by the word 'gender' in earlier cases. Since February 2023, sexual orientation and disability are written into Article 1 of the Constitution.

Since 1 July 2025 a discriminatory motive has been a statutory ground for increasing penalties in criminal cases, under a private-member's bill by Timmermans and Bikker, accompanied by expanded rights for victims and protection of victim data. Dutch legislation still contains no statutory definition of the term 'hate crime'; police record hate crimes, hate speech and other discrimination incidents through the police Centre of Expertise Discrimination (ECAD-P).

Violence risk is documented in official figures. The Dutch government reports that more than 10% of LGBTIQ+ people have experienced physical or sexual violence, including 17% of transgender people and 22% of intersex people, and that incidents of verbal abuse, intimidation and violence rose sharply according to the 2023 National Programme against Discrimination and Racism; in 2022 one third of police discrimination reports concerned sexual orientation. Police figures relayed by Transgender Netwerk and reported in April 2026 show 4,800 discrimination and violence reports about LGBTQIA+ people last year, up 7.5% on 2024 and up 81% from 2,654 in 2022, with reports concerning transgender people rising 51% in a single year, from 264 to 399. Only six convictions for anti-LGBTQIA+ discrimination were recorded last year.

Reporting infrastructure was expanded for World Pride Amsterdam, where 1.4 million visitors were expected. Amsterdam broadened its 'Safer Spaces' reporting points for anti-LGBTIQIA+ violence to cover the Nieuwe Kerk, the Stedelijk Museum, the Stadsarchief, hotels and a central RITA location. Mayor Halsema told the council that the city would tackle discrimination and violent incidents as a priority during the event, with police, enforcers and organisers agreeing to act fast. More than 70 people reported discrimination during the start of World Pride through the RITA platform, mostly festival-goers leaving the Milkshake festival and Pride Walk participants, and RITA warned that those reports are only a fraction of the total. Recent Prides drew between 25 and 45 anti-LGBTQIA+ incident reports covering vandalism, theft, discrimination, insults, intimidation and serious assault, typically with perpetrators fleeing the scene.

Facilities and legal status add to the picture. Equaldex records bathroom access as protected, non-binary people as legally recognised, discrimination as illegal with employment and housing protections on sexual orientation and gender identity grounds, and conversion therapy as banned. Same-sex marriage is legal. The Netherlands ranks 13th on the ILGA Rainbow Map 2026.

If a visitor is detained, placement rules are weak. No law, regulation or official policy governs the placement of transgender detainees; the Penitentiary Principles Act separates only male and female detainees, and the Prison Service (DJI) confirmed that placement rests on the gender designation in municipal population records (BRP) together with case-by-case factors such as gender-related physical features, the detainee's own preference, offence background and physical or mental health. Transgender detainees are frequently held on an 'Extra Care Facility' wing, generally to protect them from other detainees, alongside people with intellectual disabilities and sex offenders.
tangentialFactors:
The Netherlands sits 13th on the ILGA Rainbow Map 2026, and an international equality index ranks it second of 121 regions as a good place for LGBT people, with 52% public support for LGBT openness. Neither ranking reflects the reporting trend: recorded anti-LGBTQIA+ discrimination has climbed 81% since 2022, and convictions remain in single figures.

International monitoring of Dutch hate-crime practice notes that the country's legislation carries no statutory definition of 'hate crime', even though police record such incidents centrally through ECAD-P. The absence of a definition sits alongside the 1 July 2025 aggravating-factor rule, which increases sentences where a discriminatory motive is proven without legislating the underlying concept.

Attitudes among young people are moving in an unfavourable direction. A Utrecht University and Trimbos HBSC study found positive attitudes toward homosexuality among secondary-school boys falling from 40% to 22% and among girls from 78% to 51% between 2021 and 2025.

Open military service has applied to transgender personnel as well as gay personnel since homosexuality ceased to be classified as a mental illness in 1973.
localsOnly:
Legal gender change in the Netherlands still requires a letter from a medical expert, falling short of self-determination. The 'X' marker is available only through a court procedure that takes between three and nine months, and the Transgender Act providing self-identification was withdrawn in July 2025. Compensation has been offered to people who were sterilised under earlier rules; administrative gender recognition replaced the surgical and sterilisation requirements of the 1984-85 laws when a December 2013 law took effect in 2014.

Care for transgender adolescents is established in national guidance. The 2016 Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport guidelines, endorsed by eight medical organisations including the Dutch Psychiatry Association and Transvisie, recommend puberty blockers at Tanner Stage II with informed consent and endocrinologist approval, and top surgery is available to patients over 16. In July 2026 the Dutch Health Board reaffirmed gender-affirming care for trans youth, citing the harms of delay, mental-health improvements and a low regret rate. Conversion therapy has been excluded from health insurance coverage since June 2012 and was banned by a bill ratified on 8 September 2026.

Resident-facing protections cover employment and housing on sexual orientation and gender identity grounds, and the closure of the religious-school 'single fact' loophole in 2014 and 2015, effective 1 July 2015, means LGBTQ staff and students cannot be dismissed over sexual orientation.

The position of transgender detainees remains unsettled. The Netherlands Jurists Committee for Human Rights (NJCM) wrote to the caretaker Minister for Legal Protection, Weerwind, on 21 February 2024, describing the absence of governing rules as worrying and undesirable and noting international research documenting discrimination and sexual violence against this group, along with the relevance of CPT standards. The Dutch Institute for Human Rights and the Prison Service's practice mean outcomes depend on municipal records and individual case factors rather than on gender identity. Court decisions have treated placement on a wing that does not match a detainee's gender as making imprisonment considerably heavier: a parole-board appeals ruling of 21 March 2016 (15/4323/GB) concerned a trans woman first held in a men's institution before transfer to the women's prison at Nieuwersluis, where she reported intimidation, threats, assaults and molestation in the men's prison; the Limburg court on 17 October 2017 (ECLI:NL:RBLIM:2017:10624) considered a trans woman facing placement in a men's prison; and The Hague appeals court on 29 June 2020 (ECLI:NL:GHDHA:2020:1108) considered a trans man held in a women's prison. NJCM has asked the minister to create rules aligned with CPT standards placing detainees by gender identity.

Social conditions for LGBTQ young people include 11.4% reporting online bullying and harassment in a 2018 Statistics Netherlands survey, more than twice the rate for heterosexual young people, and a 2020 Movisie estimate of 900 to 2,000 homeless LGBTQ youth, three times the heterosexual rate, with rejection at home a stated cause.
outOfScopeNotes:
No official figures exist for the number of transgender detainees held in the Netherlands; NJCM identified this gap in its February 2024 advice, and the practice notes it described as being drafted by DIZ were unpublished at the time of writing. Whether the advice produced new placement rules is unresolved in the sources available here.

Sources conflict on the scope of hate-crime protection. The government and Equaldex record a discriminatory motive as a statutory aggravating ground from 1 July 2025, while Equaldex separately states that hate-crime protections cover sexual orientation only. Which grounds qualify for the sentence increase in practice is not resolved by the sources assembled here.

Reported incident counts capture only what is reported. RITA stated that the 70-plus World Pride reports represent a fraction of the total, and police discrimination data are compiled by a single specialist unit, so comparability across years is not established in these sources.

Equaldex describes gender change as legal but requiring a medical diagnosis while Outright International, updated March 2026, states that a medical expert letter is required; the two descriptions are consistent in substance but the exact evidentiary standard is not specified in either.
